jsonLd.headline: Strong App Alternatives in 2026, and When to Stay With Strong
jsonLd.description: Strong is free for 3 routines; Pro is $29.99 a year or $99.99 once (US App Store, Nov 2026). Why people leave, who should stay, and how Hevy and Kiron compare.

body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about Strong and Hevy comes from their App Store listings, their help pages and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Strong has been on the App Store since September 2011, and its appeal hasn't changed: it's a quick, simple way to write down a set. People who search for a Strong alternative usually aren't unhappy with the logging itself. They're stuck on something around it: the Apple Watch app, the free version's cap, or wanting an app that plans the training instead of only recording it.

That comes straight from the reviews. We went through Strong's 500 most recent US App Store reviews (May 2025 to November 2026) and counted topics by keyword, so treat the numbers as approximate. Of the 186 with 1 to 3 stars, 68 mention the Watch, 33 mention price or the paywall, and about 6 ask for things Strong was never built to do. Here's what each means for you, who should stay, and how Hevy and Kiron (that's us) compare.

Should you leave Strong?

  • Stay with Strong if you already own lifetime, your Watch syncs without trouble, or all you want is a fast log of routines you write yourself. Nothing on this page does that job better.
  • Move to Hevy if you want a free log with a little more room. Its free plan allows 4 routines to Strong's 3, and Hevy imports Strong's export file.
  • Move to Kiron if you want the app to run a plan rather than record one: a program you pick, build or paste in, with your runs on the same calendar and today's workout adjusted when time or equipment runs short. It imports your Strong history, too.

Where Kiron loses to Strong, plainly: it has no Apple Watch app, it needs a connection to open a workout, and it's newer and less proven. It also costs more: Strong Pro is $29.99 a year or $99.99 once, and Kiron is {{kiron:price-annual}}. {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}

Why people leave Strong

The Apple Watch app loses sets

The Watch is the most common complaint by a wide margin: 68 of the 186 low-star reviews. The usual story is a workout logged on the Watch, or on the Watch and phone together, that finishes with sets missing or never reaches the phone's history. Of the 16 low-star reviews that describe sets, workouts or history going missing, 11 blame the Watch sync. One reviewer in September 2026 wrote that the sync "removes sets, and even entirely fails to track my workouts."

Before you leave over it, two things. The Watch cuts both ways: 34 of the 314 four- and five-star reviews mention it too, most of them warmly. And Strong is still working on it: its October 2026 update, version 6.5.1, fixed sign-in sessions that could lapse and quietly stop syncing. If your sync broke, update, sign in again if asked, and give it a few workouts before you decide.

Three routines on the free version

Strong's free version logs unlimited workouts but keeps only 3 custom routines (the app calls them templates). Unlimited routines need Strong Pro. A push, pull and legs split fits in three; a plan with four different days doesn't. Of the low-star reviews, 33 mention price, subscriptions or the paywall, and 5 name Hevy, usually because its free plan goes further.

It records a plan; it doesn't run one

Strong does what its listing says: you write routines, pick one, and log it. It doesn't build a multi-week program, decide your next weight or plan your runs. Most Strong users like it that way. A few don't: about 6 of the 186 low-star reviews ask for a schedule, progression, plan import or better cardio. One July 2026 reviewer said Strong was falling behind newer apps, and listed Watch sync, a thin exercise library and no automatic progressive overload as the reasons.

If that's you, the real question isn't which log is better. It's whether you want an app that holds the whole plan. If you're weighing more apps than the three here, our roundup of workout apps for following a program sorts eight of them by the job they do.

Good reasons to stay with Strong

  • It's fast and simple. 103 of the 314 four- and five-star reviews use words like simple, fast, easy or intuitive. If you already know your routine, nothing gets between you and the next set.
  • The free version is real. Unlimited workouts and 3 routines, with no time limit.
  • Pro is inexpensive, and you can buy it once. It's $29.99 a year, or $99.99 for lifetime, on the US App Store. If you already own lifetime, every alternative here is new money.
  • The Watch app works for a lot of people. It logs with or without your iPhone, and plenty of reviewers keep Strong for exactly that.
  • Your data isn't locked in. Strong says you can export your data any time, as a CSV file.
  • It's mature. More than 108,000 US ratings, averaging 4.9 stars.

The App Store lists several prices for some apps, including older and alternate offers. Strong's listing also shows $3.99, $23.99 and $79.99 versions of its plans, and 6 months for $19.99. We show the prices Strong's own App Store description gives. Prices vary by country and offer.

When Hevy is the better move

Hevy is the closest thing to Strong with a roomier free plan, and for a lot of people leaving Strong it's the right answer.

  • Its free plan logs unlimited workouts and keeps up to 4 routines and 7 custom exercises, according to Hevy's help center. Independent reviews say free charts cover the last 3 months.
  • It imports Strong's file directly, and you can revert the import from the same screen if it goes wrong. Hevy's help center asks for an unedited export from Strong, in English. Routines don't come across, since Strong's file holds finished workouts only, and supersets arrive as separate exercises.
  • Hevy Pro is $23.99 a year or $74.99 once. It adds Hevy Trainer, which builds a program from your goals, equipment and schedule, and suggests weight increases. Hevy describes it as algorithm-based, not AI.
  • It has Apple Watch and Wear OS apps, a web app, and a social feed.

One caution if the Watch is your reason to leave: Hevy has Watch complaints too. 4 of its 15 low-star reviews from late October to mid-November 2026 mention the Watch. Try the free plan with your own Watch before you pay for anything. Our Hevy vs Kiron comparison covers where Hevy's free plan runs out.

When Kiron is the better move (that's us)

Kiron is built for the part Strong leaves to you: holding a plan and running it day to day. Here's what that looks like in version 1.2.

A plan from anywhere

There are four ways in: one of 36 ready-made programs, from "Beginner 5×5" to running plans like "Beginner 5K"; a program the AI builder writes from a few answers; one you build by hand; or the plan you already have. Paste that as text from ChatGPT, a coach or a website, or take a photo of it, and Kiron turns it into a scheduled program with sets, reps and rest, including plans that run in phases. PDF and spreadsheet files don't go in directly, so paste the text or use a screenshot.

The program runs on the training days you pick, on a calendar. Miss a day and Today offers to move it to a free day ("Move to Thursday", say), to pick a day yourself, or to skip it. If you've been retyping a coach's plan into Strong routines every block, that step goes away. Our guide to getting a ChatGPT plan into an app covers the pasting side.

Today's workout bends without breaking the plan

Short on time? Make today shorter: Kiron drops extras, pairs accessories into supersets, then trims accessory sets, and leaves the main lifts alone. Longer adds sets where your week is behind. In a hotel gym or the garage, switch to a saved gym and the exercises swap to what's there. You can also add core, arms or a cardio finisher, or swap an exercise for today only or from now on. Every change has Undo.

Lifting and running in one plan

Runs, rides, swims and rows sit on the same calendar as your lifts, with time and distance. A recovery map shows which muscles are still recovering, plus a cardio ring and training load, and it counts runs, rides and ski days that apps like Apple Fitness or Slopes save to Apple Health or Health Connect. When today's session leans on tired muscles, Kiron says why and offers an easier one.

Logging that feels familiar

Logging works set by set, with last time's numbers and the next weight picked from them. Warm-up sets are generated for main lifts, and there are supersets, a rest timer, a plate calculator, reps in reserve and personal records. The library has about 1,500 exercises, most with an animated demo.

Your Strong history comes with you

In Kiron, go to Settings, tap Import from another app, and choose Strong's file. Before anything is saved, you see how many workouts it holds, their date range and how many working sets. Strong's file usually doesn't say whether its weights are pounds or kilograms, so Kiron shows your heaviest set and asks. Then it lists how your exercise names match its library, with doubtful ones under "Worth a check", and you can change any of them or keep one as your own. You can remove the whole import later; workouts you logged in Kiron stay.

Where Kiron falls short

  • No Apple Watch app. Heart rate comes from Apple Health or Health Connect afterwards. If you log from your wrist, stay with Strong or try Hevy.
  • It needs a connection to open a workout, so a gym with no signal is a problem.
  • Strong wins on price. Strong Pro is $29.99 a year or $99.99 once. {{kiron:pricing-sentence}} {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}
  • No export. Kiron can't export your history as a file in version 1.2; Strong and Hevy can.
  • It's new, with a small user base, so there are no years of reviews or a community to lean on.

Moving your Strong history

Whatever you pick, take your history with you. In Strong, open Settings and tap Export Strong Data (Export Data on Android, per Strong's help center). You get a CSV file that, Strong says, can't be imported back into Strong, so keep the original somewhere safe.

  • To Hevy: Profile, Settings, Export & Import Data, Import Data, Import Strong CSV.
  • To Kiron: Settings, Import from another app, Choose file.
  • To a spreadsheet: it's one row per set, so filtering the exercise column gives you any lift's whole history. Here's our take on training from a spreadsheet vs an app.

Our guide to exporting your workout history covers Strong and five other apps, including what each file holds.

Questions people ask about leaving Strong

Is Strong free?

Yes. The free version saves unlimited workouts but is limited to 3 custom routines. Strong Pro unlocks unlimited routines and the other Pro features for $4.99 a month or $29.99 a year, or $99.99 once for lifetime (US App Store, checked November 15, 2026).

Is Strong Pro worth it?

If you like Strong and need more than 3 routines, probably. At $29.99 a year it costs less than Kiron's yearly plan ({{kiron:price-annual}}) but more than Hevy Pro ($23.99). Lifetime at $99.99 costs about the same as 3 years and 4 months of yearly Pro. If the Watch is your main reason to pay, read recent reviews first. If you want a plan run for you, Pro doesn't add that.

How do I export my workouts from Strong?

Open Strong's Settings and tap Export Strong Data, or Export Data on Android. You get a CSV file you can save, email or open in a spreadsheet.

Can I move my Strong history to another app?

Yes. Hevy imports Strong's CSV file officially, and so does Kiron, along with Fitbod and Hevy files. Other apps advertise Strong imports too. Your routines won't move anywhere, because Strong's file holds finished workouts only.

Why isn't Strong syncing with my Apple Watch?

We can't diagnose your setup, but two things are worth trying. Strong's October 2026 update (6.5.1) fixed sign-in sessions that could lapse and stop sync, so update and sign in again if asked. And several reviewers describe lost sets when logging on the phone and the Watch in the same workout, so sticking to one device per workout may help. If it still fails, contact Strong's support.

If Strong's log is fine but you want an app that runs the plan around it, try Kiron: pick or paste a plan, bring your Strong history, and see your lifting and your runs on one calendar. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron. If you just want a free log, Hevy's free plan is the better call, and it takes your Strong file too.
